paragraphs: Graph matching involves identifying corresponding nodes across graphs. This paper investigates how small, deliberately chosen changes to graph structure can undermine deep learning models that perform this task. Its focus is a vulnerability that had received less attention than attacks on other graph learning tasks, such as node classification.

The attack combines two techniques. First, it estimates node density and pushes attacked nodes toward crowded regions in both graphs. The aim is to make those nodes difficult to distinguish from their neighbors while keeping the perturbations imperceptible. Second, it uses a meta-learning approach to select starting points for projected gradient descent, improving the search for changes that damage matching quality.

Experiments on real datasets support the attack model’s effectiveness. The authors also demonstrate that attacks can transfer to other graph learning models. These findings identify a weakness involving the distinctiveness of nodes: perturbations designed to blur that distinctiveness can interfere with learned matching and may affect models beyond the original target.
neurips-2020-adversarial-attacks-on-deep.tldr: Small structural perturbations can confuse deep graph matching by making attacked nodes resemble crowded neighborhoods.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a representation for learning the three-dimensional shapes of an object category from two-dimensional images of different objects. The goal combines reconstruction with correspondence: a model should recover an object’s shape while also recognizing which points have matching identities across different instances of the category.

The Canonical 3D Deformer Map associates each image pixel with a deformation model for its corresponding 3D point. That association is canonical, meaning it is tied to the point’s identity and shared across objects. The representation brings together ideas from parametric deformation models, non-parametric reconstruction, and canonical embeddings, allowing category-wide correspondence and object-specific shape variation to be represented together.

Training requires only sparse two-dimensional supervision. At test time, the method reconstructs shape and texture from a single view and establishes dense correspondences between instances. The authors report state-of-the-art dense reconstruction results on public, in-the-wild datasets of faces, cars, and birds. These results show how shared point identities can support detailed reconstruction even when training supervision is sparse.
neurips-2020-canonical-3d-deformer-maps-.tldr: Canonical 3D Deformer Maps learn shared point identities and shape deformations to reconstruct objects from single images with sparse training supervision.

paragraphs: CircleGAN changes the discriminator in a generative adversarial network to encourage both realistic and diverse samples. Its central idea is to organize learned representations on a hypersphere, using positions relative to spherical circles to distinguish realistic examples from unrealistic ones. This gives the discriminator a geometric structure for judging generated data.

The discriminator places realistic samples around a great circle, the sphere’s longest circle, and pushes unrealistic samples toward the perpendicular poles. Longer circles offer more room for representations to spread out. The method uses this relationship between circle size and representational diversity to encourage the generator to produce varied samples as it learns to make them realistic.

For generation conditioned on class labels, the method assigns a separate hypersphere to each category and performs discrimination and updates within each class. Experiments support the approach for both conditional and unconditional generation, with state-of-the-art results on the reported standard benchmarks. The contribution is a discriminator whose representation geometry explicitly connects judgments of realism with encouragement of diversity.
neurips-2020-circlegan-generative-advers.tldr: CircleGAN organizes discriminator representations on spherical circles to encourage realistic, diverse generation.

paragraphs: Softmax converts a vector of real numbers into probabilities over categories. This paper examines how that transformation affects gradient-based optimization. The question is about the optimization behavior induced by the mapping itself: representing probabilities with softmax can create difficulties even before considering the rest of a learning system.

The authors establish two negative results. Optimizing an expectation through softmax must be sensitive to parameter initialization, a phenomenon they call the softmax gravity well. Optimizing log-probabilities through softmax must exhibit slow convergence, termed softmax damping. Their analysis uses non-uniform Łojasiewicz inequalities to derive convergence-rate bounds and explain these difficulties through the associated coefficient.

The paper then studies an alternative probability transformation called the escort mapping. It proves bounds establishing better optimization properties and supplies experimental evidence favoring the alternative. The findings make probability parameterization an explicit part of optimization design: the way numerical parameters become probabilities affects both sensitivity to starting values and the speed at which gradient-based updates make progress.
neurips-2020-escaping-the-gravitational-.tldr: The paper proves optimization drawbacks of softmax and investigates an escort mapping with better convergence properties.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering organizes data through repeated partitioning, producing groups within groups. This paper asks how to incorporate fairness into that process. It extends a notion of clustering fairness aimed at mitigating over-representation, bringing that concern into a setting where the output is an entire hierarchy rather than a single partition.

The task is to obtain a fair hierarchy while still optimizing a clustering objective. For several natural objectives, the authors develop algorithms described as simple and efficient, together with proofs that the resulting fair clusterings have good objective quality. The theoretical contribution therefore addresses both fairness and the quality of the organization produced by the algorithms.

The empirical results show fair hierarchical clusterings with only negligible losses in the objective in the tested settings. This indicates that enforcing the studied fairness notion can be compatible with maintaining clustering quality. The combination of guarantees and experiments makes the contribution broader than a fairness definition alone: it supplies practical procedures and evidence about their effect on the underlying clustering goal.
neurips-2020-fair-hierarchical-clusterin.tldr: The paper extends fairness against over-representation to hierarchical clustering and provides efficient algorithms with quality guarantees.

paragraphs: One-stage object detectors predict both object classes and bounding boxes. This paper identifies two problems in common representations: localization quality and classification can be combined inconsistently between training and inference, and representing box locations as a single concentrated point is too inflexible to capture their distribution in real data.

The proposed solution combines localization quality with the class prediction vector, so the two are learned through a joint representation. It also represents box locations with a vector describing a distribution. These changes introduce continuous training labels, which ordinary Focal Loss does not accommodate. Generalized Focal Loss extends that loss to the continuous setting so the new representations can be optimized.

On COCO test-dev, the method reaches 45.0% average precision with a ResNet-101 backbone, compared with 43.5% for SAPD and 43.6% for ATSS, at higher or comparable inference speed. The result supports changing both the prediction representation and its training objective together: the loss makes it possible to learn quality-aware class scores and more flexible box-location distributions.
neurips-2020-generalized-focal-loss-lear.tldr: Generalized Focal Loss trains joint class-quality predictions and distributed box locations, improving the reported detection accuracy without sacrificing inference speed.

paragraphs: Bayesian meta-learning aims to help a model adapt quickly to new tasks while assessing uncertainty. This paper builds on its interpretation as empirical Bayes inference in a hierarchical model. The authors first broaden that framework to encompass a variety of existing methods, then introduce a new variant based on gradient expectation-maximization.

The method separates the optimization used to adapt within a task from the meta-update that learns across tasks. This decoupling gives the inner optimization procedure more flexibility. It also avoids back-propagation computation in the meta-update step, addressing a computational burden that becomes demanding when the models involved are deep neural networks.

Experiments cover sinusoidal regression, few-shot image classification, and policy-based reinforcement learning. The authors report better accuracy with less computation and greater robustness to uncertainty. Together, these findings support the proposed separation of task adaptation and meta-updating as a way to make Bayesian meta-learning more efficient while retaining its emphasis on adaptation under uncertainty across the evaluated task types.
neurips-2020-gradient-em-bayesian-meta-l.tldr: Gradient-EM Bayesian meta-learning decouples task adaptation from meta-updates, reducing computation and improving reported accuracy and uncertainty robustness.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization seeks good solutions with relatively few evaluations, but high-dimensional search spaces can compromise that efficiency. This paper addresses problems whose search spaces have non-Euclidean geometry. It uses knowledge of that geometry to learn a smaller space in which optimization can proceed while preserving relevant structure.

The method builds on Riemannian manifolds and geometry-aware Gaussian processes. It jointly learns an embedding through nested manifolds and a model of the objective function in the resulting low-dimensional space. The acquisition function, which guides the search for evaluations, is optimized there. Learning the representation and objective together connects dimensionality reduction directly to the optimization task.

Tests on artificial benchmark landscapes show better performance than other high-dimensional Bayesian optimization approaches in several settings. The authors also report consistent optimization of the objectives, contrasting with geometry-unaware methods in those experiments. The findings support using the structure of non-Euclidean domains as useful information when reducing the dimensionality of a search problem, rather than treating all parameter spaces identically.
neurips-2020-high-dimensional-bayesian-o.tldr: Geometry-aware Bayesian optimization learns low-dimensional manifold representations to improve search in high-dimensional non-Euclidean spaces.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations describe computation through continuous dynamics, offering a continuous-depth approach to neural networks. Their practical use can be restricted by the cost of solving those equations. This paper targets that computational bottleneck, aiming to make prediction with continuous-depth models competitive in time with traditional discrete networks.

The authors introduce hypersolvers: neural networks designed to solve ordinary differential equations with low overhead. The approach combines these learned solvers with Neural ODEs and includes theoretical guarantees on accuracy. Its central contribution concerns the machinery used to evaluate continuous dynamics, making the equation-solving step part of the effort to improve practical model efficiency.

Experiments on standard benchmarks, including sampling from continuous normalizing flows, report consistent Pareto efficiency relative to classical numerical methods. That finding concerns the tradeoff between computational cost and solution accuracy. The reported results support hypersolvers as a route to cheaper inference for continuous-depth models, with the theoretical analysis supplying accuracy guarantees alongside the empirical efficiency comparisons.
neurips-2020-hypersolvers-toward-fast-co.tldr: Hypersolvers are learned ODE solvers that combine low inference overhead with accuracy guarantees for continuous-depth models.

paragraphs: Online rent-or-buy problems require decisions before the full future is known. This paper studies them as sequential decision-making problems and asks how predictions, typically supplied by machine learning, can improve those decisions. Its focus is on combining predictive information with algorithms whose performance can still be analyzed when the predictions are inaccurate.

The authors consider two specific problems: ski rental and dynamic TCP acknowledgment. They develop new online algorithms within the sequential framework and derive explicit performance bounds in terms of prediction accuracy. This makes the quality of the forecast part of the mathematical performance statement, connecting the usefulness of prediction to the decisions the algorithm makes over time.

The algorithms approach optimal performance when predictions are accurate while hedging against less accurate forecasts. The contribution is therefore both algorithmic and analytical: it provides ways to use predictions and describes how performance depends on their reliability. The stated findings support prediction-assisted online decision-making without requiring every prediction to be treated as dependable.
neurips-2020-improving-online-rent-or-bu.tldr: New rent-or-buy algorithms exploit accurate predictions while bounding performance in terms of prediction error.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student network using a teacher’s soft outputs, which convey more than a single class label. Although this approach has worked for model compression and knowledge transfer, its theoretical explanation has been less developed. This paper studies distillation in wide neural networks through a neural tangent kernel approximation.

That approximation represents the network as a linear model built from its random features. Within this linearized setting, the authors derive a transfer risk bound and introduce data inefficiency, a measure of how difficult a task is to learn from data. The measure provides a way to analyze how the choice of training targets affects learning.

For a perfect teacher, the analysis shows that using a high proportion of soft labels can be beneficial. For an imperfect teacher, hard labels can correct erroneous teacher predictions. These findings explain why combining hard and soft labels can be useful: the teacher provides guidance, while ground-truth labels can counter its mistakes. The conclusions are developed through the paper’s wide-network, linearized analysis.
neurips-2020-knowledge-distillation-in-w.tldr: A linearized analysis of wide networks explains when teacher soft labels help and how hard labels can correct an imperfect teacher.

paragraphs: Learning objectives often reduce many numbers to one value. A model may combine losses across training examples or combine prediction scores across labels. This paper introduces the sum of ranked range as a general way to perform that aggregation, making the ordering of values part of how the objective is constructed.

The procedure sorts a set of real numbers and sums a consecutive portion of the resulting sequence. A ranked range therefore specifies which positions in the ordering contribute to the objective. The authors solve the resulting minimization problem using the difference of convex algorithm, providing an optimization approach alongside the proposed form of aggregation.

The paper develops two applications: an AoRR aggregate loss for binary classification and a TKML individual loss for multi-label or multi-class classification. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the applicability of these losses and the effectiveness of the optimization framework. The shared contribution is a way to formulate objectives at two different levels, across examples and across labels, using the same ranked-range principle.
neurips-2020-learning-by-minimizing-the-.tldr: The sum of ranked range builds learning objectives by aggregating consecutive portions of sorted losses or scores.

paragraphs: User-level differential privacy protects all observations belonging to one person, a stronger requirement than protecting an individual item. This paper studies how many users are needed to estimate a distribution over k symbols when each user contributes m samples. The goal is to understand how additional samples per person can help under that privacy requirement.

For straightforward Laplace or Gaussian mechanisms, the required user count has a statistical term proportional to k/(mα²) and a privacy term proportional to k/(εα), where α measures estimation error and ε controls privacy. More samples improve the statistical term but leave this privacy penalty unchanged. The paper also establishes a same-order requirement for mechanisms restricted to operating on the final aggregate.

The proposed mechanism reduces the privacy term to roughly k/(√m εα), ignoring logarithmic factors, in specified settings. It is nearly optimal in certain regimes, yielding a roughly square-root-of-m improvement in the privacy penalty. The paper also develops lower-bound techniques. Its findings show that how user data is processed can determine whether additional samples improve privacy-constrained estimation.
neurips-2020-learning-discrete-distribut.tldr: A user-private distribution estimator can reduce the privacy penalty by roughly √m in certain settings by going beyond final-aggregate mechanisms.

paragraphs: Distributed stochastic gradient descent can use compressed messages or delayed updates, creating several related optimization problems. This paper develops a unified analysis covering quantized, error-compensated, and delayed-update variants. A single theorem supplies complexity results for methods within the framework, matching the best-known results for existing methods covered by the analysis.

The framework also generates new methods combining error feedback and quantization with variance reduction or arbitrary sampling. The authors present sixteen new variants and derive improved convergence rates. One method, EC-SGD-DIANA, combines error feedback for biased compression with quantization of gradient differences, connecting two ways of managing information lost or transmitted during distributed updates.

When workers compute full gradients, EC-SGD-DIANA approaches the exact optimum asymptotically in expectation with a constant learning rate for convex and strongly convex objectives. For worker losses expressed as finite sums, the authors introduce EC-LSVRG-DIANA, a stochastic method combining error feedback and variance reduction with the same stated type of exact asymptotic convergence. These qualifications distinguish the guarantees from claims of exact finite-time optimization.
neurips-2020-linearly-converging-error-c.tldr: A unified analysis yields new compressed distributed SGD methods, including constant-learning-rate methods with exact asymptotic convergence in expectation under stated conditions.

paragraphs: Distribution alignment attempts to bring different data distributions into agreement, with applications including domain adaptation and unsupervised image translation. This paper addresses weaknesses in two common approaches: simple statistical distances can miss complex distribution structure, while adversarial alignment can be difficult to train and lacks automatic quantitative validation and universal convergence guarantees.

The proposed method combines normalizing flows with a log-likelihood ratio statistic. Together, they define a neural likelihood-based minimization objective. Under certain assumptions, the authors show that this objective reaches a known lower bound upon convergence. Having a known target value gives the optimization an explicit quantitative reference for assessing its result.

Experiments verify that minimizing the objective produces alignment while preserving local structure within the input domains. This supports the usefulness of the objective beyond merely making distributions agree according to a numerical score. The theoretical result remains conditional on its assumptions and on convergence; it supplies a characterized endpoint, while the experiments provide evidence that the learned alignment retains local relationships in the evaluated data.
neurips-2020-log-likelihood-ratio-minimi.tldr: Normalizing flows and a log-likelihood ratio yield a distribution-alignment objective with a known lower bound under stated assumptions.

paragraphs: An adaptive controller must learn a system’s dynamics while choosing actions from incomplete observations. This is difficult because its own decisions introduce correlations into the data it collects. The paper introduces a model-estimation method with finite-time guarantees for both open-loop and closed-loop identification of partially observable linear dynamical systems.

The authors use this estimator in AdapOn, an algorithm that learns the dynamics and repeatedly updates its controller. It occasionally fits a linear regression model using interactions with the environment. A re-parameterized policy and the estimated dynamics then produce counterfactual loss functions, which support controller updates through online gradient descent. Improving model estimates makes the gradient updates more accurate over time.

The analysis bounds regret after T interactions by a polylogarithmic function of T. This establishes slow growth of cumulative performance shortfall in the studied adaptive-control setting. The authors identify AdapOn as the first algorithm known to them with this guarantee for unknown, partially observable linear systems, including linear quadratic Gaussian control. The result connects finite-time system estimation with a long-run control guarantee.
neurips-2020-logarithmic-regret-bound-in.tldr: AdapOn combines system estimation and online controller updates to obtain polylogarithmic regret for unknown partially observable linear systems.

paragraphs: Filling missing entries in a table produces estimates, but those estimates can differ substantially in reliability. This paper introduces a probabilistic matrix-completion framework that provides both imputed values and uncertainty for each one. It addresses the gap between reconstructing a complete dataset and knowing how much confidence to place in its reconstructed entries.

The Low Rank Gaussian Copula model extends probabilistic principal component analysis with a separate marginal transformation for each column. Those transformations let the model better match the distributions of different variables. The framework handles Boolean, ordinal, and real-valued observations, while model-fitting time scales linearly with the number of rows and the number of columns.

Experiments report state-of-the-art imputation accuracy across varied data types, including high-rank data. The uncertainty estimates also carry useful information: entries assigned lower uncertainty have lower error on average. For real-valued data, the reported confidence intervals are well calibrated. These results support uncertainty as an informative companion to the completed table, while preserving the distinction between average reliability and correctness of every individual estimate.
neurips-2020-matrix-completion-with-quan.tldr: A Low Rank Gaussian Copula model fills mixed-type missing data and supplies uncertainty estimates that track imputation error.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent chooses actions from observations that may differ from the true state because of measurement errors or adversarial noise. This paper studies how to make agents robust to such distortions. The authors find that directly applying classification-oriented defenses, including naive adversarial training, is ineffective for many reinforcement learning tasks.

They introduce the state-adversarial Markov decision process to analyze this problem and derive a policy regularization approach from that framework. The regularization applies to a broad family of deep reinforcement learning algorithms, including DDPG, PPO, and DQN. Its scope includes control tasks with both discrete and continuous actions, linking the theoretical formulation to several established learning methods.

Experiments show substantial robustness improvements for those three algorithms under a suite of strong white-box attacks, including two attacks introduced by the authors. Robust policies also improve performance in a number of environments. These findings support treating observation robustness as a reinforcement learning problem in its own right, with a defense tied to policy behavior and sequential decision-making.
neurips-2020-robust-deep-reinforcement-l.tldr: A state-adversarial decision framework yields policy regularization that improves reinforcement learning robustness to corrupted observations.

paragraphs: Self-training methods can work under larger domain shifts than much existing theory explains. This paper analyzes a specific shift in which some features predict labels in the source domain but become independent of labels in the target domain. Such features provide source-specific shortcuts that an adapting classifier should stop using.

The theory considers linear classifiers, Gaussian spurious features, and non-spurious features drawn from a mixture of log-concave distributions. Under this setting, entropy minimization on unlabeled target data avoids the spurious feature when initialized with a sufficiently accurate source classifier. The guarantee is notable because the optimization objective is non-convex and has multiple undesirable local minima that use the spurious features.

Experiments on semi-synthetic Celeb-A and MNIST tasks verify the theory for the studied type of shift. The authors suggest that collecting diverse data and self-training on it may help reduce classifier biases even when labeling is impractical. That practical suggestion follows from a conditional result: the proof concerns a specified feature distribution and requires a decently accurate starting classifier.
neurips-2020-self-training-avoids-using-.tldr: Under specified distributional and initialization conditions, self-training on unlabeled target data provably avoids spurious source-domain features.

paragraphs: Attention mechanisms often distribute weight over a finite set of items. Sparse alternatives to softmax can assign zero weight to irrelevant items, allowing the set of attended categories to vary. This paper extends that idea to continuous domains, where attention can describe regions of a continuum instead of only individual categories.

The authors extend alpha-entmax to continuous distributions and establish connections with Tsallis statistics and deformed exponential families. They also construct continuous-domain attention mechanisms and derive efficient gradient backpropagation algorithms for alpha values of one and two. These contributions connect the distributional formulation to the computations needed to train neural networks using it.

Experiments in text classification, machine translation, and visual question answering illustrate one-dimensional and two-dimensional continuous attention. The mechanisms can attend to time intervals and compact spatial regions. The results demonstrate a different way to represent what a model attends to, extending sparse attention’s variable-support idea beyond finite lists and showing its use in several attention-based learning tasks.
neurips-2020-sparse-and-continuous-atten.tldr: The paper extends sparse probability mappings to continuous domains, enabling trainable attention over intervals and compact regions.

paragraphs: When several people speak simultaneously, a microphone array records a mixture of their voices. This paper jointly tackles two tasks: determining where the speakers are and separating their speech. The method does not require the number of speakers in the recording to be known in advance.

Its core is a neural network that operates directly on waveforms and isolates sound sources inside a specified angular window. The inputs include a direction of interest and the width of the region around it. Repeatedly shrinking that width exponentially enables a binary search that localizes and separates sources in logarithmic time, tying the separation procedure to spatial refinement.

At test time, the algorithm accommodates an arbitrary number of potentially moving speakers, including more speakers than appeared during training. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance for both separation and localization, particularly under high background noise. The findings show how a direction-selective network can be reused within a search procedure to address recordings whose speaker count and locations vary.
neurips-2020-the-cone-of-silence-speech-.tldr: A direction-selective waveform network uses progressively narrower angular windows to locate and separate an unknown number of speakers.

paragraphs: Pruning removes neural network parameters, but it can also improve test accuracy despite greatly reducing model size. This paper investigates that improvement by studying pruning during training. It defines pruning instability as the immediate drop in test accuracy caused by a pruning step, separating that short-term disruption from later generalization benefits.

Across a wide variety of pruning settings, the authors find that greater instability accompanies larger improvements in generalization. They propose that pruning acts similarly to noise injection, regularizing the training process through the disturbance it creates. Supporting evidence includes an association between lower pruning stability and flatter models, along with benefits that do not require permanent parameter removal.

The findings provide an explanation for why pruning can improve generalization even though highly overparameterized networks can also generalize well. On the proposed account, the training disturbance matters alongside any reduction in model size. This is an empirically supported mechanism across the studied settings, rather than a claim that every larger accuracy drop will necessarily produce a better final model.
neurips-2020-the-generalization-stabilit.tldr: Across studied settings, more disruptive pruning brings larger generalization gains, supporting a noise-like regularization explanation.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much of a trained neural network’s information lies in the placement of its weights. The authors observe that weight locations carry most of the information encoded by training in their investigation. They hypothesize that the locations and exact numerical values of weights can be treated as separate dimensions.

To test that hypothesis, they introduce lookahead permutation, or LaPerm, which trains networks by reconnecting weights. With random dense initial weights, it achieves speed and performance similar to or better than conventional optimizers such as Adam. With random sparse weights containing many zeros, reconnection changes which neurons are linked and achieves accuracy comparable to a well-trained dense network.

When initial weights share a single value, LaPerm finds a weight-agnostic network with accuracy far above chance. These experiments provide evidence that connectivity can carry substantial learned information across several initialization settings. The contribution is both a training method and an empirical test of the separation hypothesis; the results support the importance of weight arrangement without establishing that exact values are universally irrelevant.
neurips-2020-train-by-reconnect-decoupli.tldr: LaPerm trains networks by reconnecting weights, providing empirical evidence that weight locations carry substantial learned information.

paragraphs: An image can receive high likelihood from a generative model even when its objects differ from those in the training data. This paper explains the problem in invertible networks through model bias and shared image properties. Low-level features learned across natural-image datasets dominate likelihood, making anomalies defined by high-level features such as shape harder to detect.

The first proposed remedy compares log likelihoods from two otherwise identical models trained on the target distribution and a broader image distribution. An additional outlier loss uses samples from the broader distribution to improve detection. The second remedy uses only the final-scale likelihood contribution of a multiscale model, because earlier scales mainly capture low-level features.

The final-scale approach is especially useful when a suitable broader image distribution is unavailable. Overall, the methods achieve strong unsupervised anomaly detection and slightly underperform leading classifier-based methods in the supervised setting. The findings connect detection performance to which levels of visual information dominate the score, and provide two ways to reduce interference from shared low-level image structure.
neurips-2020-understanding-anomaly-detec.tldr: Likelihood ratios and final-scale scoring improve image anomaly detection by reducing the influence of shared low-level features.

paragraphs: Weighted sampling supports statistical estimation and compact representations of data. When weights are highly uneven, repeatedly drawing the same heavily weighted items can limit coverage. This paper develops sketches for sampling without replacement, which provides broader representation and higher accuracy than sampling with replacement for the same sample count under skewed weight distributions.

The sketches implement ℓp sampling, weighting keys by a power p between zero and two of their frequency or accumulated signed updates. They are composable, and their size grows only linearly with the requested sample size. The design uses existing heavy-hitter sketches such as CountSketch, giving the construction a practical basis despite the complexity of its analysis.

The authors identify their method as the first to support without-replacement sampling for p greater than one and the first to handle signed updates for positive p. These extensions broaden the kinds of weighted data that compact sketches can sample. The contribution combines increased sampling coverage with a representation whose size scales directly with the number of samples requested.
neurips-2020-wor-and-p-s-sketches-for-el.tldr: Composable sketches enable weighted sampling without replacement across p values from zero to two, including new support for signed updates.
